title: Non-text Content
sourceQuote: All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, except for the situations listed below.
publisherCheck: Inventory every piece of non-text content presented to users (images, image text, icons, charts, image buttons, form images, media, CAPTCHAs, canvas/SVG graphics). For each item, decide which case applies and confirm with a human judgement: (1) general content has a text alternative serving the equivalent purpose in context; (2) controls or inputs have a name describing their purpose; (3) time-based media, tests or exercises invalid as text, and sensory-experience content have at least a descriptive identification; (4) CAPTCHAs have text identifying and describing their purpose plus an alternative CAPTCHA form using a different sensory output mode; (5) pure decoration, visual-only formatting, or content not presented to users is implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.
evidenceNeeded: A per-item inventory listing location, the case assigned (general, control/input, time-based media, test, sensory, CAPTCHA, decoration/formatting/invisible), the exact text alternative or accessible name as exposed to assistive technology, and the reviewer's reasoning on equivalence of purpose in context. For CAPTCHAs, record the alternative output modes offered. For items treated as decorative, record how they are hidden from assistive technology and why they carry no information.
failureExample: A product page shows a bar chart image of monthly prices whose only text alternative is "chart", so a screen reader user cannot get the figures the chart conveys; the alternative does not serve the equivalent purpose.
limitation: This card records a manual review plan only; status remains not-assessed and no website was evaluated. Presence of alt attributes or names in source or automated scan output cannot establish that an alternative serves the equivalent purpose, that an item is truly decorative, or which exception applies; that requires human judgement in context. Additional requirements for controls (4.1.2) and media (Guideline 1.2) are out of scope of this card.

title: Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded)
sourceQuote: An alternative for time-based media is provided that presents equivalent information for prerecorded audio-only content
publisherCheck: Inventory every prerecorded audio-only item (for example podcasts, voice recordings) and video-only item (for example silent animations, screen recordings without sound). For each audio-only item, confirm an alternative for time-based media is provided that presents equivalent information. For each video-only item, confirm either an alternative for time-based media or an audio track presenting equivalent information is provided. Have a reviewer compare the full media against its alternative for missing information. Record any item treated under the exception only when it is a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such, citing the text it duplicates and the label.
evidenceNeeded: A media inventory listing each prerecorded audio-only and video-only item with its location and classification; for each item, the linked or adjacent alternative (transcript, text description, or audio track) and a human reviewer's note comparing it to the complete media for equivalent information; for each exception claim, the text the media duplicates and the visible label identifying the media as an alternative for that text.
failureExample: A recipe page embeds a silent video-only clip showing each preparation step, with no text alternative or audio track; the steps shown are not described anywhere else, so information in the clip is unavailable to people who cannot see it.
limitation: This card supports manual publisher review only. Source inspection or automated tools can detect media elements and linked files, but cannot confirm that an alternative presents equivalent information or that an exception label is clear; live and synchronized media are outside this criterion. No website was evaluated, so no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance is asserted.

title: Captions (Prerecorded)
sourceQuote: Captions are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media
publisherCheck: Inventory every prerecorded synchronized media item the publisher presents (audio or video synchronized with another format or with time-based interactive components). For each item that is not a clearly labeled media alternative for text, play it end to end and confirm captions are available, stay synchronized with the audio, convey the spoken dialogue, identify speakers where needed, and include the non-speech audio information (such as sound effects or music) needed to understand the content. For each item excluded as a media alternative for text, confirm it presents no more information than text already on the page and that the page clearly labels it as such.
evidenceNeeded: A list of each prerecorded synchronized media item with its location; for each, how captions are provided (closed track or open/burned-in) and the reviewer's notes from a full playback comparing captions to the audio for completeness, timing, speaker identification and needed non-speech information; for each claimed media-alternative-for-text exception, the equivalent text it duplicates and the visible label that identifies it.
failureExample: A product tutorial video on a help page ships an auto-generated caption track that omits a narrator's spoken warning and never indicates the alert tone that signals an error state the viewer must recognize.
limitation: This card is a manual review aid, not a conformance result. Source inspection or automated tools can show that a caption track or file exists, but they cannot establish that captions are accurate, complete, synchronized, or include needed non-speech information, nor that an exempt item really adds no information beyond its text and is clearly labeled; a human must review each media item in playback. Live media is outside this criterion and is covered separately by 1.2.4 Captions (Live).

title: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded)
sourceQuote: An alternative for time-based media or audio description of the prerecorded video content is provided for synchronized media
publisherCheck: Inventory every prerecorded synchronized media item (video with an audio track) the publisher controls. For each item, a human watches the full item and confirms that either an audio description of the prerecorded video content or an alternative for time-based media is provided and reachable alongside it. If the item is claimed to be a media alternative for text, confirm the equivalent text exists and the media is clearly labeled as such; only then does the exception apply.
evidenceNeeded: Per item: its location and identity, whether it is prerecorded synchronized media, which option is provided (audio-described version or description track, or a time-based media alternative document) and where a user finds it, reviewer notes from watching the item against that option, and for any exception claim the referenced text and the visible label stating the media is an alternative for that text.
failureExample: A prerecorded product demo video shows on-screen steps and settings values that the narration never speaks, and the page offers no audio-described version and no text alternative for the video.
limitation: This card records packet readiness only, not WCAG conformance; no website was evaluated. Detecting a description track, transcript link, or label in source or by automated tooling does not show that the description or alternative conveys the important visual content; that requires human review of each item. Live media and audio-only or video-only media are outside this criterion, and this card does not assess other media criteria.

title: Captions (Live)
sourceQuote: Captions are provided for all live audio content in synchronized media
publisherCheck: Inventory every place the site presents live synchronized media with audio (for example webcasts, live-streamed events, live video meetings published as page content). For each, a human reviewer confirms during an actual live session that captions are available for the live audio, stay synchronized with it, and convey the speech plus non-speech audio information needed to understand the content (speaker identification, relevant sounds). Record which sessions were observed and when.
evidenceNeeded: Per live stream: the page URL and player used; how captions are delivered (open captions, or closed captions with a user-visible way to turn them on); the captioning source (for example a human real-time captioner or other caption feed); dated reviewer notes or recordings from at least one observed live session showing captions present, synchronized, and covering speech and needed non-speech audio. Note whether the stream is live under the WCAG definition (real-world event, no more than a broadcast delay).
failureExample: A library streams its monthly author talk live on its events page. The embedded player shows video and audio of the speaker and audience questions, but no caption track or open captions are provided during the broadcast; a caption file is only added to the archived recording days later.
limitation: Live captioning can only be judged by a human observing actual live sessions; source code, player configuration, or automated scans cannot show that captions were present, synchronized, or adequate during a broadcast, and one observed session does not establish other sessions. Scope follows WCAG definitions: wholly computer-generated content is not live, and media that is a clearly labeled media alternative for text is not synchronized media. Prerecorded media belongs to 1.2.2. This card records review readiness only and makes no conformance claim.

title: Audio Description (Prerecorded)
sourceQuote: Audio description is provided for all prerecorded video content in synchronized media
publisherCheck: List every prerecorded (not live) video that is combined with audio or time-based interaction. Leave out media that only repeats information already in text and is clearly labeled as a media alternative for text. For each remaining item, watch it with the audio on and the picture covered. Note each important visual detail, such as actions, characters, scene changes, or on-screen text, that the main soundtrack does not convey. Then confirm that a narrated description of those details is available: in the main soundtrack, as a selectable described audio track, or as a described version of the same video. Narration added in existing dialogue pauses is enough here; extended (paused-video) description is not required by this criterion. A video whose existing audio already carries all of its visual information needs no added description.
evidenceNeeded: A media inventory with URLs or file names, durations, and whether each item is prerecorded. For any item treated as a media alternative for text, the text it duplicates and the visible label. For each item, a reviewer log listing the important visual details and the timestamps where the described audio conveys them, or a note that the existing audio already carries them. The name of the described track or described version, and how users reach it from the page where the original video plays. The reviewer name, review date, and media version reviewed.
failureExample: A product-launch video shows a presenter pointing to on-screen price and release-date captions while saying only 'here's what you've been waiting for'. No described track or described version exists, so a listener cannot get the price or date.
limitation: This card guides a human review and records no result. No website or media was evaluated. A captions file, a transcript, a player 'AD' toggle, or a track-kind attribute in the source does not show that the narration covers the important visual details, so automated or source-only checks cannot establish conformance. A transcript alone meets 1.2.3, not 1.2.5. Live video falls under no prerecorded-media criterion here. Extended audio description (1.2.7) is AAA and out of scope.

title: Info and Relationships
sourceQuote: Information, structure , and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text.
publisherCheck: For each page or screen in scope, list every piece of information, structure, and relationship that the visual presentation conveys (for example headings, lists, table header-to-cell associations, form label-to-field pairings, grouped controls, required-field or emphasis cues). For each item, confirm it is either exposed in the markup or accessibility tree so software can determine it, or stated in text; record which of the two routes applies.
evidenceNeeded: A reviewer-made inventory pairing each presentational cue with its programmatic exposure (element, role, or association observed in the source or accessibility tree) or the text that states it, plus screenshots or notes showing the presentation being matched and the reviewer's name and date.
failureExample: A shipping form shows 'Name' and 'Postcode' as visually adjacent text beside inputs, and marks required fields only with bold labels, but the inputs have no associated labels and the required state is neither exposed programmatically nor stated in text.
limitation: This card records manual review readiness only; no website was evaluated. Source inspection or automated checks can show some structure is present but cannot establish that every relationship conveyed through presentation was identified, so they do not demonstrate that the criterion is met.

title: Meaningful Sequence
sourceQuote: When the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning, a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined
publisherCheck: For each page or document under review, first identify content whose order affects meaning (for example step-by-step instructions, a heading followed by its body text, a label followed by its value, a question followed by its answer choices, multi-column articles). Where order does not affect meaning, record that judgement and its reason. Where it does, compare the visually presented order with the order exposed programmatically (DOM or source order for web content, tag/reading order for documents) and record whether a correct reading sequence is available there. Note any spots where visual position was produced by layout techniques such as CSS positioning or reordering, layout tables, or spaces/tabs used to form columns, and check each against the programmatic order.
evidenceNeeded: A list of the reviewed pages or documents with the specific regions where sequence affects meaning; for each region, the visually presented order (a screenshot or written description) alongside the programmatic order (a DOM/source-order excerpt, an accessibility-tree or linearized-text export, or a document tag-order listing), plus the reviewer's name, date, and the tool or method used to obtain the programmatic order. Mismatches need the exact element or tag reference.
failureExample: A recipe page shows numbered preparation steps in the correct visual order, but the markup lists step 3 before step 1 and uses CSS positioning to place it lower on screen, so a screen reader announces the steps out of order and the instructions no longer make sense.
limitation: This card prepares a manual review and records evidence only; no website or document has been evaluated, so it asserts no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance. Whether a sequence affects meaning and whether an exposed order is 'correct' are human judgements: more than one order can be correct, and source scanning or automated tools cannot decide either question alone. This criterion concerns reading sequence, not keyboard focus order, which is a separate criterion.

title: Sensory Characteristics
sourceQuote: Instructions provided for understanding and operating content do not rely solely on sensory characteristics of components such as shape, color, size, visual location
publisherCheck: Inventory every instruction the content gives for understanding or operating it (form hints, error messages, tutorials, help text, prompts, audio cues). For each one, check whether the component it refers to can be identified only by shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound. If so, check whether the same instruction also identifies the component by something that does not depend on that sense, such as its visible text label, name, or heading.
evidenceNeeded: A list of instructions with their location (page, screen, or step), the exact instruction wording, the component each one refers to, the sensory characteristics it uses, and any non-sensory identifier given alongside them. Include screenshots or transcripts that show the instruction next to the component it refers to.
failureExample: A checkout form says "Press the round green button on the right to continue", and the button's only label is an arrow icon. A user who cannot see its shape, color, or position cannot tell which control the instruction means.
limitation: This applies only to instructions for understanding and operating content. It forbids relying solely on sensory characteristics, not mentioning them; "Select the Continue button on the right" is acceptable. Color-only meaning in general is covered under Guideline 1.4, not here. A source or automated scan cannot judge what an instruction means or what it refers to, so human review of rendered content is required. This card makes no conformance claim.

title: Orientation
sourceQuote: Content does not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation, such as portrait or landscape, unless a specific display orientation is essential
publisherCheck: For each page, screen, and interactive state in scope, view it in portrait and in landscape display orientation and confirm the content is neither locked to one orientation nor hidden, blocked by a 'rotate your device' message, or made inoperable in the other. Review the publisher's own CSS orientation media queries, manifest orientation settings, and script orientation locks for any restriction. For each restriction found, record which content it affects and the publisher's reason, and check that reason against the WCAG definition of essential: removing the orientation would fundamentally change the information or functionality, and it cannot be achieved another way that would conform.
evidenceNeeded: A list of the pages, views, and states reviewed; human-reviewed captures or notes of each in portrait and in landscape showing that content and controls remain viewable and operable; an inventory of any orientation media queries, manifest orientation values, or orientation-lock calls found in the publisher's code with the affected content; and, for each retained restriction, a written rationale explaining why that specific orientation is essential.
failureExample: A recipe site's step-by-step cooking view uses an orientation media query to replace the steps with a 'Please rotate your phone to portrait' overlay whenever the device is held in landscape, so a reader with a tablet mounted sideways on a stand cannot read or advance the steps, even though nothing about the recipe requires portrait.
limitation: Packet readiness only; no website was evaluated, so this criterion is not assessed. Finding orientation code in source does not prove a restriction, and finding none does not prove content works in both orientations; both orientations must be reviewed by a human in rendered content. Whether an orientation is essential is a human judgment against the WCAG definition; the Note's examples (bank check, piano application, projector or television slides, virtual reality content) are cases where it may be essential, not automatic exemptions. The criterion concerns restrictions imposed by content; an orientation lock the user sets on their own device is outside what this check can attribute to the publisher.

title: Identify Input Purpose
sourceQuote: The purpose of each input field collecting information about the user can be programmatically determined
publisherCheck: List every form input field in scope. Mark each field that collects information about the user (not about another person) and whose purpose matches an entry in the WCAG 2.2 'Input Purposes for User Interface Components' section. For each marked field, confirm in the rendered markup that its purpose is exposed programmatically through a mechanism the implementing technology supports (for HTML, an autocomplete attribute whose token corresponds to that listed purpose). Record which fields were judged outside the criterion and why: not about the user, purpose not in the list, or technology lacking support.
evidenceNeeded: Per-form inventory naming each field, its visible label, whether it collects information about the user, the matching listed input purpose (or none), and the rendered attribute or other programmatic exposure observed; identification of the implementation technology and whether it supports identifying expected meaning for form input data; the rendered DOM or markup actually served (not only templates or design files) for every form state reviewed.
failureExample: An account sign-up form in HTML has fields labelled 'Email' and 'Phone' for the user's own contact details, but the inputs carry no autocomplete attribute or an unrelated token, so the purpose (email, tel) cannot be programmatically determined.
limitation: Applies only to fields collecting information about the user whose purpose is in the WCAG listed input purposes, and only when the technology supports identifying expected meaning. Correct markup does not show browser or assistive-technology behaviour; source-only or automated attribute scans cannot establish which fields concern the user or confirm conformance. No website was evaluated.

title: Use of Color
sourceQuote: Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.
publisherCheck: For each page or screen in scope, list every place where color carries meaning: conveyed information (status, categories, chart series, required or invalid fields), indicated actions (links within text, selected or active controls), prompts for a response, and visual elements that must be told apart. For each, confirm a non-color visual cue also carries that meaning, such as text, a label, an icon, a pattern, a shape, underlining, or position. Viewing the item in grayscale is one way to check whether the meaning survives without hue.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of the color-coded items reviewed, with the meaning each color carries and the non-color visual cue that duplicates it (or a note that none was found). Include screenshots of each item in normal color and in grayscale, plus the states that were checked (default, hover, focus, selected, error).
failureExample: A sign-up form marks invalid fields only by turning their borders red. There is no error text, icon, or other visual change, so a user who cannot tell red from the default border color cannot see which fields need fixing.
limitation: This card records a manual review and does not evaluate any website. Source inspection or automated tools cannot tell when color is the only cue, because they cannot judge what a color means to a reader. A human has to interpret each use of color in its rendered context. This criterion does not set any contrast ratio and lists no exceptions. The normative wording covers visual means only; the informative note sends programmatic access to color and other visual coding to Guideline 1.3. Completing this card does not establish conformance.

title: Audio Control
sourceQuote: If any audio on a web page plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, either a mechanism is available to pause or stop the audio
publisherCheck: On each page in scope, list every source of audio that starts without a user action, including embedded video, background music, and third-party widgets. Time how long each one plays. For any audio that plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, confirm one of two things: a mechanism on the page pauses or stops it, or a mechanism on the page controls its volume independently from the overall system volume level. Check every piece of content on the page, including content not relied on to meet other criteria, because the criterion's note applies it to all content under Conformance Requirement 5: Non-Interference.
evidenceNeeded: A per-page inventory of each automatically playing audio source, its observed play duration, and whether it exceeds 3 seconds. For each source over 3 seconds, a record of which mechanism is provided (pause/stop, or independent volume control), where it is on the page, and a reviewer note confirming that a human operated it and it stopped the audio or changed its volume without changing system volume. Record the reviewer, date, and page version.
failureExample: A product landing page autoplays a 30-second promotional video with sound, and the embedded player has its controls hidden, so the page has no way to pause, stop, or lower that audio other than the device's system volume.
limitation: This card supports manual review only; it records no pass or fail result. Source inspection or automated scanning cannot establish how long audio plays at runtime, whether a script or third-party embed starts audio, or whether a mechanism actually works and is independent of system volume, so a human must observe the rendered page. Audio that plays automatically for 3 seconds or less is outside this criterion's requirement, and the card makes no claim about other criteria or about overall WCAG conformance.

title: Contrast (Minimum)
sourceQuote: The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1
publisherCheck: Inventory every text and image-of-text presentation, including states such as hover, focus, error and overlays. For each one, record the foreground color and the specified background it renders over in normal use. Compute the WCAG contrast ratio (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) from relative luminance. Require at least 4.5:1, or at least 3:1 for large-scale text (at least 18 point, or 14 point bold, or the CJK equivalent, measured at delivered size before any user resizing). Exempt only text that is part of an inactive user interface component, pure decoration, not visible to anyone, part of a picture containing significant other visual content, or part of a logo or brand name, and record why each exemption applies.
evidenceNeeded: A per-item table listing the location, state, foreground and background color values, font size and weight as delivered, the computed ratio, the threshold applied (4.5:1 or 3:1), and any exemption claimed with its justification. For text over images or gradients, include the sampled background region and how it was chosen. For images of text, include the image asset and the sampled colors. Record that the review covered both text color and background color being specified together.
failureExample: A help article shows 16px regular-weight caption text in #999999 on a white #FFFFFF background. That is about 2.85:1, below the 4.5:1 required for text that is not large-scale.
limitation: This card is a review aid; no website was evaluated, and no pass, fail, inapplicability or conformance is claimed. Source-only or automated color checks cannot settle this criterion on their own: they miss text rendered over images, gradients or dynamic states, cannot judge whether an exemption such as decoration, inactive component or logotype really applies, and cannot confirm the delivered font size and weight. A human must verify the rendered presentation.

title: Resize Text
sourceQuote: text can be resized without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality.
publisherCheck: For each page or view in review scope, a human reviewer enlarges text to 200 percent using means that do not require assistive technology (for example the user agent's zoom or text-size setting, or a text-resizing control the page itself provides), then confirms that all text content remains present and readable and that every function available at default size (links, form controls, menus, dialogs, buttons) can still be perceived and used. Captions and images of text are excluded from this check; other text, including text inside controls, labels, tooltips and error messages, is in scope.
evidenceNeeded: A record per reviewed page or state naming the browser and version, the resizing method used, and the resize level reached (200 percent), with paired screenshots or notes at default size and at 200 percent showing whether any text was clipped, truncated, overlapped or hidden and whether each interactive function was still operable; plus a note of which visible text items were treated as captions or images of text and therefore excluded.
failureExample: When browser zoom is set to 200 percent, a fixed-height navigation bar clips its menu labels and pushes the 'Submit' button of a contact form behind a non-scrollable overlay, so the form can no longer be submitted without returning to default size.
limitation: This card records a manual review procedure only; status stays not-assessed and no website was evaluated. Source inspection or automated scanning (for example spotting fixed pixel font sizes) cannot by itself establish pass or fail, because the criterion concerns observed loss of content or functionality at 200 percent. The criterion requires resizing to work without assistive technology, so success through a screen magnifier alone does not demonstrate it; captions and images of text are excepted by the criterion text, and this card does not add requirements beyond 200 percent or for reflow, which is separately covered by 1.4.10.

title: Images of Text
sourceQuote: If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text
publisherCheck: List every image, canvas, SVG raster, background image, or embedded media frame that renders text to achieve a visual effect, including buttons, headings, banners, quotes, menus, and scanned notices. Exclude text that is only part of a picture containing significant other visual content, such as a name tag in a photograph. For each remaining item, record whether the page's technologies (for example HTML text styled with CSS and web fonts) can achieve the same visual presentation. Where they can, confirm the information is conveyed as real text rather than an image of text unless an exception applies: Customizable, meaning the user can visually customize the image of text to their requirements (for example font, size, color, background); or Essential, meaning that particular presentation of text is essential to the information conveyed. Logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) are considered essential. Record the claimed exception and its rationale per item.
evidenceNeeded: A human-reviewed inventory of each image of text with its page location, the text it shows, a screenshot or asset reference, and the image's purpose; for each item, a note on whether the visual presentation is achievable with the technologies in use; for any claimed Customizable exception, a record of the user-facing customization mechanism and which visual properties it changes; for any claimed Essential exception, a written rationale (or identification as a logotype); and the reviewer name and date.
failureExample: A product page's section headings and a promotional 'Free shipping over $50' banner are exported as PNG images using a web-available font and plain background, so the same appearance could be produced with HTML text and CSS; no exception applies because the images cannot be visually customized and the presentation is not essential.
limitation: This card guides manual review only and records no result for any website. Source inspection or automated tools can locate image assets but cannot decide whether rendered text is an image of text, whether the technologies could achieve the presentation, or whether the Customizable or Essential exception applies; those are human judgments. Text alternatives for these images are a separate criterion (1.1.1) and do not satisfy this one. Packet readiness never means WCAG conformance.

title: Reflow
sourceQuote: Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions
publisherCheck: For each page and state under review, a human views vertically scrolling content at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels (for example a 1280 CSS pixel wide viewport at 400% zoom) and content designed to scroll horizontally, such as vertical text, at a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels (for example a 1024 CSS pixel tall viewport at 400% zoom). The reviewer confirms that all text, controls, menus, dialogs and other information remain present and usable without scrolling in both directions, and separately records any parts claimed to require two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning, such as images required for understanding (maps, diagrams), video, games, presentations, data tables (not individual cells), or interfaces that must keep toolbars in view while manipulating content.
evidenceNeeded: Per reviewed page and state: the starting viewport size and zoom level (or equivalent CSS width or height) used, browser and operating system, screenshots or recordings at that size showing whether a second scroll direction appears, a list of any information or functionality that is hidden, clipped, overlapping or unreachable, and for each section exempted as requiring two-dimensional layout, its location and the reason its usage or meaning depends on that layout.
failureExample: At a 1280 CSS pixel wide viewport zoomed to 400%, an article page keeps a fixed-width 960 CSS pixel text column, so readers must scroll horizontally to read each line of paragraph text while also scrolling vertically through the article.
limitation: This card records what a human must check; it does not assess any website. Source review, CSS inspection or automated tools cannot alone establish that information and functionality survive at the stated sizes, and whether a section truly requires two-dimensional layout is a human judgment. Allowing two-dimensional scrolling within an excepted part does not excuse the rest of the page. Completing this card does not establish WCAG 2.2 conformance.

title: Non-text Contrast
sourceQuote: The visual presentation of the following have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s)
publisherCheck: Inventory the user interface components and graphics on the pages in scope. For each component, identify the visual information required to identify the component and each of its states (for example boundaries, focus indicators, selected or checked marks, icon-only controls) and measure its contrast ratio against adjacent color(s); record any ratio below 3:1. For each graphic, identify the parts required to understand the content (for example chart lines, data markers, meaningful icon strokes) and measure them against adjacent color(s) the same way. Then apply the criterion's exceptions per item: inactive components; component appearance determined by the user agent and not modified by the author; and graphics whose particular presentation is essential to the information being conveyed. Record each exception claim with its reason rather than skipping the item.
evidenceNeeded: Per item: page URL or screen, the component or graphic and the state examined (default, hover, focus, selected, checked, error as applicable), the identifying visual part measured, the foreground and adjacent color values actually rendered with the measured contrast ratio and the tool or method used, and, where an exception is claimed, which exception applies and why (for example evidence the component is inactive, or that default user-agent styling is unmodified by author CSS). Rendered measurements are required because author styles, images, gradients and overlays determine the adjacent colors; source color tokens alone do not establish them.
failureExample: A sign-up form styles its text inputs with a 1px light-grey border (#DDDDDD) on a white background and no other visual boundary or fill; the border is the only visual information identifying the input, and its contrast ratio is about 1.4:1, below 3:1.
limitation: This card supports human manual review only and records no result; no website was evaluated, so no claim of pass, fail, inapplicability or conformance is made. Automated or source-only checks cannot decide which visual information is required to identify a component or state, which graphic parts are required to understand the content, or whether an exception applies, and they may miss states, gradients, images or overlays that change the adjacent colors.

title: Text Spacing
sourceQuote: no loss of content or functionality occurs by setting all of the following and by changing no other style property
publisherCheck: For each page template and content type implemented in a markup language supporting these text style properties, have a reviewer apply all four overrides at once, changing no other style property: line height at least 1.5 times the font size, spacing following paragraphs at least 2 times the font size, letter spacing at least 0.12 times the font size, and word spacing at least 0.16 times the font size. Compare against the unmodified rendering and confirm no text is clipped, truncated, overlapped, or hidden, and no control, menu, form field, tooltip, or dialog becomes unusable. Where a language and script does not use one or more of these properties, record which properties exist for that combination and check only those, as the stated exception permits.
evidenceNeeded: A list of reviewed templates and states (including expanded menus, form errors, and dialogs) with the language/script of each; the exact override values or stylesheet used and confirmation that it changed no other style property; paired before/after captures per template; a per-item note of any lost content or functionality; and, for any script relying on the exception, a written rationale naming the properties that do not exist for that language and script.
failureExample: A navigation button sets a fixed pixel height with overflow hidden; once line height and letter spacing are increased to the required values, the second line of its label is cut off and the user can no longer read the button's purpose.
limitation: This card records a manual review procedure only; no website has been evaluated. The criterion does not require content to use these spacing values, only that user overrides cause no loss, so source review or automated style scans cannot establish the outcome; it depends on rendered behaviour under the overrides for each page and state. Outcomes for content outside the reviewed templates, or not implemented in a supporting markup language, remain unknown.

title: Content on Hover or Focus
sourceQuote: Where receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, the following are true
publisherCheck: List every author-controlled tooltip, sub-menu, popover or similar content that appears when a trigger receives pointer hover or keyboard focus and hides when that hover or focus is removed. Exclude content whose visual presentation is controlled by the user agent and not modified by the author, such as the browser tooltip for an HTML title attribute. For each remaining instance, check three things. Dismissible: with the pointer or focus still on the trigger, confirm that a mechanism, such as pressing Escape, dismisses the content. This is not required if the content communicates an input error or does not obscure or replace other content. Hoverable: if hover can trigger the content, move the pointer from the trigger onto the content and confirm that it stays visible. Persistent: confirm that the content stays visible until the trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid, with no timeout.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of hover and focus triggered content instances, with page, trigger and type. For each instance, record whether author code or the user agent controls its presentation, the dismissal mechanism tested with the trigger still active, the pointer-onto-content result where hover applies, and whether it ever disappears on its own. Also record whether the content reports an input error or obscures or replaces other content, and keep human tester notes or a recording with the user agent and input method used.
failureExample: On a product page, hovering over a help icon shows a custom tooltip that covers the adjacent price text. The tooltip closes when the pointer moves toward it, so its long text cannot be magnified or read under the pointer. Escape does not close it while the icon keeps hover or focus.
limitation: This card is a manual review checklist only. Source code, CSS or automated scans cannot show whether content stays visible while the pointer moves onto it, whether it ever disappears on its own, or whether the dismissal mechanism works across user agents and input methods. That requires human interaction testing. Hidden components shown on focus, such as skip links, are not additional content. Completing this card does not declare the criterion passed, failed, inapplicable or conformant.

title: Keyboard
sourceQuote: All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes
publisherCheck: Inventory every function the content offers (links, buttons, form controls, menus, dialogs, carousels, media controls, drag-and-drop, custom widgets). With the pointer unused, a reviewer operates each function through a keyboard interface only, confirming it can be reached and activated, and that no step depends on how fast or how long an individual key is pressed. For any function relying on the path exception, record why the underlying function (not merely the input technique) requires path-dependent input rather than just endpoints.
evidenceNeeded: A dated list of the functions reviewed, with the page/state, the keys used to reach and operate each one, and the observed outcome; notes on any keystroke-timing requirement found; for each claimed path-dependent exception, the function, the reason its underlying function depends on the user's movement path, and the reviewer's name. Pointer-only handlers, scripts, or tool output alone are not sufficient evidence.
failureExample: A product image gallery lets visitors reorder favourites only by dragging thumbnails with a mouse; no keyboard-operable alternative (such as move-up/move-down buttons) exists, so reordering cannot be done through a keyboard interface even though the underlying function only needs start and end positions.
limitation: This card guides manual review only; no website was evaluated and nothing here states the content passes, fails, or conforms. Source inspection or automated scanning cannot confirm that all functionality is keyboard operable or that the path exception applies. The exception concerns the underlying function, not the input technique (handwriting text input is not exempt), and providing mouse or other input methods in addition to keyboard is not forbidden.

title: No Keyboard Trap
sourceQuote: focus can be moved away from that component using only a keyboard interface, and, if it requires more than unmodified arrow or tab keys
publisherCheck: List every component on each page that keyboard focus can reach, including embedded players, iframes, widgets, rich-text editors, dialogs and third-party content. For each one, a human reviewer moves focus into the component with the keyboard only, then tries to move focus out with unmodified Tab, Shift+Tab, arrow keys or other standard exit methods. If leaving needs anything more, the reviewer confirms that the user is told the exit method. All content on the page is in scope, even content that is not used to meet other criteria.
evidenceNeeded: A per-page inventory of focusable components, including embedded and third-party content. For each component: the keys used to enter and leave it, the result (focus left or stayed trapped), and the browser, assistive-technology and platform used. Where a non-standard exit is needed: the exact wording and location of the advice telling users how to move focus away, captured as a screenshot or transcript. Record the reviewer's name and the review date.
failureExample: A page embeds a third-party video player. Once focus enters the player, Tab and Shift+Tab only cycle through its play, volume and fullscreen buttons. Escape does nothing, and no instructions explain how to return to the rest of the page. A keyboard-only user cannot reach the content after the player.
limitation: This card only prepares a manual review and is not an assessment. Source inspection and automated tools cannot show whether focus can actually leave a component at runtime, especially for scripted widgets, plugins or iframes. Any trap anywhere on the page affects the whole page under the Non-Interference conformance requirement. No pass, fail, not-applicable or conformance claim can be made without hands-on keyboard testing of the rendered content.

title: Character Key Shortcuts
sourceQuote: If a keyboard shortcut is implemented in content using only letter (including upper- and lower-case letters), punctuation, number, or symbol characters
publisherCheck: List every keyboard shortcut the content itself implements. For each one, record whether it fires on a single letter (any case), punctuation, number, or symbol key with no modifier key such as Ctrl or Alt. For each such shortcut, confirm at least one of these holds: a mechanism turns it off; a mechanism remaps it so it includes one or more non-printable keys such as Ctrl or Alt; or it is active only while its own user interface component has focus. Shortcuts that already require a non-printable key, and shortcuts that belong to the browser, operating system, or assistive technology rather than the content, are outside this criterion's condition.
evidenceNeeded: A complete inventory of content-implemented shortcuts, each with its trigger key(s), the component or page it is scoped to, and which of the three options (turn off, remap, active only on focus) applies. For turn off or remap, the location and steps of the mechanism and a human observation that it takes effect. For active only on focus, a human observation that the key does nothing while focus is elsewhere, including while typing in a text field. Record the content version or date the inventory covers.
failureExample: A webmail page archives the open message whenever the user presses the single key "e" anywhere on the page, offers no setting to disable or remap it, and listens at document level, so a speech input user dictating text outside an edit field triggers archiving.
limitation: This card prepares a manual review and records no outcome. Source code or automated scans can surface key listeners but cannot prove the shortcut inventory is complete, that a disable or remap mechanism actually works, or that a shortcut is truly scoped to focus; a human must observe the running content. No website has been evaluated, so no pass, fail, not-applicable, or conformance claim may be made from this card.

title: Timing Adjustable
sourceQuote: For each time limit that is set by the content, at least one of the following is true
publisherCheck: List every time limit the content itself sets (session timeouts, timed forms, auto-advancing steps, timed redirects or refreshes). For each one, record which single option applies: Turn off (user can turn it off before encountering it); Adjust (user can adjust it before encountering it over a wide range at least ten times the default); Extend (user is warned before expiry, given at least 20 seconds to extend with a simple action, and can extend at least ten times); or one of the Real-time, Essential, or 20 Hour exceptions, with the reason the exception holds. Flag any time limit for which no option or exception is recorded for human follow-up.
evidenceNeeded: A human-compiled inventory of content-set time limits with each limit's default duration; for each, a manual walkthrough note or recording showing the turn-off or adjust control is reachable before the limit is encountered, or the warning, the time given to respond (at least 20 seconds), the simple extend action, and that extension works at least ten times; for any claimed exception, a written justification (real-time event with no possible alternative, essential limit whose extension would invalidate the activity, or duration over 20 hours).
failureExample: A benefits application form signs the user out after 15 minutes of inactivity with no prior warning, no way to extend, and no setting to turn off or lengthen the timeout, and the timeout is not part of a real-time event, essential, or longer than 20 hours.
limitation: Source review or automated scanning can locate timers in code but cannot show that a turn-off, adjust, or extend mechanism works for users, that warnings arrive before expiry, that 20 seconds and ten extensions are actually available, or that an exception legitimately applies; those need human judgement on the rendered content. This card records a review prompt only and makes no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance determination for any website.

title: Pause, Stop, Hide
sourceQuote: there is a mechanism for the user to pause, stop, or hide it or to control the frequency of the update
publisherCheck: Inventory every moving, blinking, scrolling, or auto-updating item on each page in scope (carousels, marquees, animated banners, tickers, live feeds, auto-refreshing widgets), including third-party embeds and decorative animation. For each moving, blinking, or scrolling item, record whether it starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds, and is presented in parallel with other content; for each auto-updating item, record whether it starts automatically and is presented in parallel with other content. Where those conditions hold, confirm a user-operable mechanism exists to pause, stop, or hide the item (or, for auto-updating content, to control update frequency), and record any claim that the movement or updating is part of an activity where it is essential with its justification for human review.
evidenceNeeded: Per page: a list of each moving, blinking, scrolling, or auto-updating item with its location and origin (first-party or embedded); observed start behavior and duration of motion; whether it runs alongside other content; the identity, location, and operation of any pause, stop, hide, or update-frequency control, observed by a human reviewer in the rendered page; and a written rationale for each item claimed to be essential.
failureExample: A homepage news carousel starts rotating on load, advances every four seconds indefinitely beside the main article text, and offers only previous/next arrows with no control to pause, stop, or hide the rotation.
limitation: This card is a manual-review prompt only; no website was evaluated and nothing here establishes that any page passes, fails, or is exempt. Source review or automated scans cannot confirm runtime start behavior, duration, parallel presentation, a working control, or whether motion is essential. Flickering or flashing content is addressed by Guideline 2.3, not this card; per the criterion's notes, all content on the page is in scope under Conformance Requirement 5 (Non-Interference), and content updated or streamed while paused need not be preserved.

title: Three Flashes or Below Threshold
sourceQuote: Web pages do not contain anything that flashes more than three times in any one second period
publisherCheck: Inventory every item on each page that can flash: video, animation, animated images, canvas or CSS effects, transitions, ads and third-party embeds, including content not relied on to meet any other criterion. For each item, confirm no one-second period contains more than three flashes; otherwise confirm the flashes are below the general flash and red flash thresholds as defined in the WCAG 2.2 glossary.
evidenceNeeded: Per-page list of flashing items with location and source; frame-accurate timing or playback recording showing the maximum flashes in any one-second window; where more than three, the threshold analysis output (tool name, version, settings, display assumptions) for general and red flash; reviewer name and date.
failureExample: A product launch page autoplays an embedded promo video whose intro uses a full-frame white strobe flashing about five times per second, and no general or red flash threshold analysis exists for it.
limitation: Source or markup review cannot show rendered flash rate, area, or red content; automated scanners cover only part of this. This card records a manual review procedure only; no website was evaluated and no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance claim is made.

title: Bypass Blocks
sourceQuote: A mechanism is available to bypass blocks of content that are repeated on multiple web pages
publisherCheck: List the blocks of content the publisher repeats across multiple web pages (for example site header, primary navigation, sidebars, cookie or promo banners placed before main content). For each such block, identify the mechanism the publisher relies on to let users bypass it, and confirm by manual review of representative page templates that the mechanism is present and reaches past that block to the content that follows.
evidenceNeeded: A reviewer-recorded inventory of repeated blocks per page template, the named bypass mechanism for each (with its location in the page), and a dated note of the manual walk-through showing the mechanism was operated and where it led, plus the page URLs or template identifiers reviewed.
failureExample: Every article page begins with the same 40-link navigation menu, and a "Skip to content" link exists in the markup but points to an id that no longer exists after a template change, so activating it does not move past the menu.
limitation: This card records publisher review readiness only; status stays not-assessed and no website was evaluated. The saved criterion text does not name a required mechanism, so the presence of a particular technique in source code or an automated scan result does not by itself show the criterion is met or failed; a human must judge which blocks repeat across pages and whether the mechanism actually bypasses them.

title: Page Titled
sourceQuote: Web pages have titles that describe topic or purpose.
publisherCheck: For each web page in the review scope, a human reviewer records the title the page exposes (for HTML, the title element text as shown in the browser tab or history), then judges whether that title, read on its own, describes the topic or purpose of that particular page's content rather than only the site, a template placeholder, or a file name.
evidenceNeeded: A page inventory listing each in-scope web page URL or identifier, the exact title text captured from the rendered page, a one-line summary of that page's main topic or purpose, and the reviewer's note on whether the title describes it, with reviewer name and review date.
failureExample: Every page of a recipe site, including the lentil soup recipe and the contact form, exposes the same title "Home - Example Recipes", so a user switching tabs cannot tell which page covers which topic or purpose.
limitation: Packet readiness only: this card records that a human review is needed and is not-assessed; no website was evaluated. Checking source code or running an automated tool can show that a title exists, but cannot decide whether it describes the page's topic or purpose, so neither establishes conformance. The saved normative text requires description of topic or purpose only; this card adds no uniqueness or length requirement.

title: Focus Order
sourceQuote: focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability
publisherCheck: First record whether the page can be navigated sequentially and whether the navigation sequence affects meaning or operation; the criterion applies only when both hold. Then, for each page state in scope (including opened menus, dialogs, disclosed content, and form steps), move focus forward and backward through every focusable component using sequential navigation alone, and judge whether the order in which components receive focus preserves the meaning and operability of the content.
evidenceNeeded: A reviewer's written record naming the pages and states covered, the sequential navigation method and user agent used, the observed focus sequence for each state, and a human judgment, with reasons, on whether that sequence preserves meaning and operability; plus a note of any state where the applicability conditions were judged not to hold.
failureExample: A checkout form lets users tab from the card-number field to the footer links and back to the expiry and security-code fields, so the sequence interrupts a task whose fields must be completed together.
limitation: This card records packet readiness only and assesses no website. Source inspection, tabindex values, or automated tools cannot show whether a focus sequence preserves meaning and operability; that needs human judgment of the rendered states, so no pass, fail, or conformance claim follows from this card.

title: Link Purpose (In Context)
sourceQuote: The purpose of each link can be determined from the link text alone or from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context
publisherCheck: List every link on each page in scope, including image links, icon-only links, and links inside repeated components. For each link, record its accessible link text (visible text, image alt text, or an accessible name such as aria-label) and decide whether a reader can tell where the link goes or what it does from that text alone. Where the text alone is not enough, check whether the purpose is clear when combined with programmatically determined link context: the same sentence, paragraph, list item, or table cell, or a heading or table header that is programmatically associated with the link. Treat context as acceptable only if it is exposed in the markup, not merely placed visually nearby. Record a link under the exception only when its purpose would be ambiguous to every user, including users who can see the surrounding page, and write down why.
evidenceNeeded: Per page: an inventory of links with each link's accessible text, its destination or action, and the specific programmatic context relied on (enclosing sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell, or associated heading/header), captured from rendered markup and accessibility-tree inspection by a human reviewer; notes on image and icon-only links showing their text alternative; and written justification for any link placed under the 'ambiguous to users in general' exception.
failureExample: A product listing repeats a 'Read more' link under each item, each pointing to a different product page, and the product name sits in a separately styled block that is not in the same sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell, or programmatically associated heading as the link, so the link's purpose cannot be determined from its text or programmatic context.
limitation: This card records publisher review steps only; status stays not-assessed and no website has been evaluated. Source-code reading or automated tools can flag generic link text but cannot judge whether text plus programmatic context conveys purpose, or whether the 'ambiguous to users in general' exception applies; that needs human judgment on the rendered page. Meeting this criterion does not establish 2.4.9 Link Purpose (Link Only) or overall WCAG conformance.

title: Multiple Ways
sourceQuote: More than one way is available to locate a web page within a set of web pages
publisherCheck: Identify the set of web pages under review and, separately, any pages that are the result of, or a step in, a process. For each remaining page, record at least two distinct ways a user can locate it within that set (for example navigation menu plus site search, site map, or table of contents), and confirm each way actually reaches that page rather than only the home page.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of the pages in the set; per page, the two or more locating mechanisms with where they appear and the path each gives to the page; a list of pages excluded as process results or process steps, with the process each belongs to and why the exclusion applies.
failureExample: A product documentation site reachable only through a nested sidebar menu: it has no search, no site map, and no other pages link to its articles, so the sidebar is the single way to find any given article.
limitation: Packet readiness only; no website was evaluated. Whether two mechanisms are genuinely distinct, whether pages form one set of web pages, and whether the process exception applies are human judgments; source review or automated crawling cannot by itself establish conformance. The criterion concerns locating pages within a set, not navigation within a single page, and does not mandate any particular mechanism.

title: Headings and Labels
sourceQuote: Headings and labels describe topic or purpose.
publisherCheck: Inventory every heading and every label presented to users on each page and state (form field labels, button and link text acting as labels, section and region labels, other text or text-alternative components identifying a component; not only HTML label elements). For each, a human reviewer reads it in context and records whether it describes the topic of the content it introduces or the purpose of the component it identifies, checking that repeated identical headings or labels on one page are distinguishable where their topics or purposes differ.
evidenceNeeded: Per page and state reviewed: the list of headings and visible labels with their location, the content or component each one introduces or identifies, the reviewer's judgment and rationale for each, the scope (pages, templates, dynamic states) covered, plus reviewer name and date.
failureExample: A checkout form labels its two address blocks only as "Section 1" and "Section 2", and an order-notes field carries the visible label "Field 7", so none of these headings or labels describes the topic or purpose of what it introduces.
limitation: The normative text is one sentence; it concerns headings and labels that are present and does not itself demand headings be added, nor that they be programmatically marked up (other criteria address structure and names). Descriptiveness is a contextual human judgment: source review or automated heading/label detection can find empty or duplicate text but cannot establish that text describes topic or purpose. This card records a not-assessed review item, not a pass, fail, inapplicability or conformance claim for any website.

title: Focus Visible
sourceQuote: Any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible.
publisherCheck: Using only the keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, and the keys each widget expects), move focus through every keyboard-operable component on each page in scope, including menus, dialogs, custom widgets, and embedded content. Confirm that every focused component shows a visible keyboard focus indicator. If the indicator only appears in a particular mode, such as an author-provided setting, confirm that the mode exists, can be reached, and shows focus on every component.
evidenceNeeded: A list of the pages, states, and keyboard-operable components that were reviewed. For each component, a screenshot or short recording of it receiving keyboard focus with the indicator visible. The browser, operating system, and any assistive technology or display settings used. A description of any mode that has to be turned on to show focus, and how a user reaches it. Any component where focus could not be seen, with steps to reproduce.
failureExample: A site stylesheet removes the focus outline from links and buttons (for example with outline: none) and nothing replaces it. A keyboard user tabbing through the navigation menu cannot tell which link will activate when they press Enter.
limitation: This card records a manual review step and has not been assessed. Reading source code or running automated tools cannot show that focus is visible for every component, in every state, under the conditions users actually have, so a clean packet check is not a conformance claim. This criterion only requires that some mode with a visible focus indicator exists. It does not set minimum size, contrast, or freedom from being hidden behind other content; those belong to other criteria (2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), 2.4.13 Focus Appearance) and are not evaluated here.

title: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
sourceQuote: When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component is not entirely hidden due to author-created content.
publisherCheck: A human reviewer moves keyboard focus forward and backward through every focusable user interface component on each page and state the publisher owns, including while author-created sticky headers, sticky footers, cookie or consent banners, chat launchers, non-modal dialogs and overlays are displayed. At each stop, record whether any part of the focused component remains visible or whether author-created content entirely hides it. Per the informative notes of the pinned section, consider only initial positions of user-movable content, and treat content the user opened as not obscuring when the user can reveal the focused component without advancing keyboard focus; record which case applied.
evidenceNeeded: Per page and state reviewed: the list of focusable components traversed, the keyboard sequence used, the viewport size and zoom level, which author-created persistent or overlaying content was present, and a screenshot or note for each stop where the focused component was partly or wholly covered stating whether some part stayed visible. For user-opened content, record whether the component could be revealed (for example by dismissing the content) without moving focus.
failureExample: An author-created sticky cookie-consent banner fixed to the bottom of the viewport stays open while the user tabs through an article; when focus moves to a link in the last visible line, the page does not scroll it clear and the banner entirely covers the link.
limitation: This card supports a manual publisher review only; no website has been evaluated and status is not-assessed. Source inspection or automated scanning cannot establish the outcome, because whether a component is entirely hidden depends on rendered layout, viewport, zoom, scroll position and runtime state. Partial obscuring is not addressed by this criterion's wording, and the notes cited in publisherCheck are informative under WCAG 2.2, not additional requirements. No pass, fail, inapplicability or conformance is claimed.

title: Pointer Gestures
sourceQuote: All functionality that uses multipoint or path-based gestures for operation can be operated with a single pointer without a path-based gesture
publisherCheck: List every feature where the page's own scripts interpret multipoint gestures (pinch, two-finger swipe or rotate) or path-based gestures (swipe, drawn shapes). For each one, confirm the same function also works with one pointer and no path: for example a single tap or click on a button, link, or step control. If no such alternative exists, record whether the publisher claims the gesture is essential and the reason given. Leave out gestures that only operate the browser, operating system, or assistive technology.
evidenceNeeded: A per-feature inventory naming the gesture, the function it performs, and the single-pointer, non-path alternative (control name and location) or the written essential-gesture rationale. Add screenshots or a short recording of a human activating each alternative with a single tap or click, plus the browser, device, and input type used.
failureExample: A product image carousel moves between photos only by horizontal swipe, and its map widget zooms only by two-finger pinch. There are no previous/next or zoom-in/zoom-out buttons, so a user who can only tap with one finger or a head pointer cannot reach later photos or zoom.
limitation: This card is a review prompt. It does not evaluate any website. Reading the source code or running automated scanners cannot show that every gesture-driven function has a working single-pointer alternative, or that a claimed essential exception holds; a human must check both. The criterion applies only to pointer actions interpreted by web content, not to actions needed to operate the user agent or assistive technology. Dragging movements are reviewed separately under 2.5.7. This card makes no pass, fail, applicability, or conformance determination.

title: Pointer Cancellation
sourceQuote: The down-event of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function
publisherCheck: List every function on the page that a person can operate with a single pointer (click, tap, or stylus press), including custom controls, drag-and-drop, sliders, and canvas or game controls. For each one, press the pointer down on it and stop. Note whether anything happens before release, such as navigation, submission, deletion, a purchase, playing media, or a state change. If nothing happens until release, the function meets the No Down-Event option. If something does happen on press, check whether at least one of the other options holds: (a) the function completes only on release, and the person can abort it before completion (for example, by moving the pointer off the target before releasing) or undo it afterwards; (b) releasing the pointer reverses whatever the press did, as with press-and-hold previews that disappear on release; or (c) completing on press is essential. Under the saved Note 1, functions that emulate a keyboard or numeric keypad key press count as essential. Also repeat the press-then-move-off-and-release test on drag targets.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of the single-pointer functions that were reviewed. For each function, a record of which event triggers it: press (down-event) or release (up-event). Where the function fires on press, record which option applies: the abort-or-undo mechanism and how it works, the up-reversal behavior that was observed, or a written rationale for why completing on press is essential, such as a keyboard or keypad emulation. Name the reviewer, date, and the browsers, pointer types, and assistive technology configurations that were used. Where useful, attach the relevant event-handler code or a screen recording as supporting evidence. Code alone does not show runtime behavior.
failureExample: A shopping page has a custom 'Remove item' button scripted to delete the cart line on mousedown or pointerdown. A user who presses it by accident cannot slide the pointer away to cancel, and no undo or restore option is offered. The item is gone before the pointer is released.
limitation: This card is a manual-review prompt only. No website has been evaluated, and it records no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance outcome. Static source or automated scanning can flag down-event handlers, but it cannot settle the criterion. Only human operation shows whether an abort, undo, or up-reversal option actually works, or whether completing on press is essential. The saved Note 2 limits the criterion to web content that interprets pointer actions. Actions needed to operate the user agent or assistive technology are excluded. Keyboard-only operation is out of scope here.

title: Label in Name
sourceQuote: For user interface components with labels that include text or images of text , the name contains the text that is presented visually.
publisherCheck: List every user interface component whose visible label includes text or images of text. For each one, record the visible label text exactly as presented, then record the programmatically determined name exposed by the rendered page. Confirm that the name contains the visible label text. Components without a visible text or image-of-text label are outside this criterion's scope.
evidenceNeeded: Per component: a screenshot or transcription of the visible label text, including text rendered inside images; the accessible name observed in the rendered page through an accessibility-tree or assistive-technology inspection; and the markup or attribute that supplies that name, such as aria-label, aria-labelledby, alt, or a label element.
failureExample: A button visibly reads "Send", but its aria-label is "Submit form", so the exposed name does not contain the visible word "Send" and a speech-input user saying "click Send" cannot activate it.
limitation: This card records a publisher's manual review checklist only; no website was evaluated. Source inspection alone cannot show the computed accessible name or the visually presented label, and automated tools cannot confirm which text is the visible label, so no conformance claim follows from this card. The note recommending that the label text start the name is non-normative.

title: Motion Actuation
sourceQuote: operated by device motion or user motion can also be operated by user interface components and responding to the motion can be disabled
publisherCheck: List every function the content triggers from device motion (for example shaking, tilting, or orientation events) or from user motion detected by a sensor or camera (for example gestures toward a camera). For each one, confirm that a user interface component can operate the same function, and that the content's response to the motion can be turned off to prevent accidental actuation. Record a function as an exception only if the motion operates it through an accessibility supported interface, or if the motion is essential and replacing it would invalidate the activity, and write down the reason.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of motion-triggered functions with the triggering motion, its sensor or API source, and where it appears. For each function: the equivalent user interface component and how to reach it, how motion response is disabled (a setting or control) and whether the disabled state holds, plus any claimed Supported Interface or Essential exception and its justification. Include a human reviewer's notes from real devices where the motion was performed.
failureExample: A recipe page lets readers shake their phone to undo clearing a shopping list, but provides no on-screen undo button. The shake response also cannot be switched off, so the list gets cleared by accident when the reader walks with the phone.
limitation: This card is a publisher review aid only. No website was evaluated, and this card does not establish that any content passes, fails, or is exempt from 2.5.4. Code inspection or automated scans cannot reliably find every motion listener or confirm working alternatives, disable controls, or exception claims. Deciding whether an interface is accessibility supported, or whether a motion is essential, needs human judgment on real devices.

title: Dragging Movements
sourceQuote: All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential
publisherCheck: List every author-implemented function that is operated by dragging, such as sortable lists, sliders, drag-to-upload zones, map panning, and kanban cards. For each one, try to reach the same result with a single pointer that does not drag, for example tap or click controls, click-to-select then click-to-place, or step buttons. Record the alternative that was found or note that none was found. Treat a function as exempt only when there is a documented reason that dragging is essential, or when the behavior is provided by the user agent and the author has not modified it. Do not count gestures that operate the browser or assistive technology itself.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of drag-operated functions with their page or component locations. For each function, a recorded single-pointer non-dragging procedure that a reviewer actually performed, with the outcome compared against the dragging result, for example a screen recording or step notes. A written rationale for any claim that dragging is essential, and confirmation of whether any user-agent-native drag behavior was modified by author code.
failureExample: A task board lets users move cards between columns only by press-hold-and-drag. There is no move menu, column selector, or click-to-place option, so a person who uses a single pointer but cannot hold and drag cannot reorder their tasks.
limitation: This packet card is a manual-review prompt, not a conformance result. No website was evaluated, and source inspection or automated scans cannot show whether a non-dragging single-pointer path really achieves the same function. Whether dragging is essential, and whether user-agent behavior was modified, are human judgments that need evidence. Keyboard operability alone does not satisfy this pointer-specific criterion.

title: Target Size (Minimum)
sourceQuote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels
publisherCheck: For each page, list every pointer target (links, buttons, icons, form controls, custom widgets) and record its rendered size in CSS pixels. For any target under 24 by 24 CSS pixels, record which exception the publisher relies on: Spacing (a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle centered on each undersized target's bounding box intersects no other target and no other undersized target's circle); Equivalent (another control on the same page performs the same function and meets the criterion); Inline (the target is in a sentence or its size is constrained by the line-height of non-target text); User Agent Control (the user agent sets the size and the author has not changed it); or Essential (that presentation is essential or legally required for the information conveyed). Mark any undersized target that has no documented exception for human follow-up.
evidenceNeeded: Per page and state reviewed: the target inventory with rendered width and height in CSS pixels and how they were measured; for each undersized target, the exception claimed and its support, such as a spacing-circle diagram, the identity and location of the equivalent control, the surrounding sentence or line-height for inline targets, confirmation that no author styling is applied to user-agent-sized controls, or the legal or informational basis for an essential presentation; and the viewport, zoom level, and interaction states (hover, open menus, dialogs) that were covered.
failureExample: A toolbar of 16 by 16 CSS pixel icon buttons with 2 CSS pixels between them, where the spacing circles of neighbouring buttons intersect and the page has no other control for the same actions, has no applicable exception, so a reviewer should flag it.
