limitation: This packet records review steps only; no website was evaluated, so nothing here says the criterion is passed, failed, not applicable, or conformant. Source or CSS reading alone cannot show rendered target size, overlap, or spacing, which depend on layout, viewport, zoom, fonts, and states. Automated measurement cannot judge whether the Equivalent or Essential exceptions apply. The saved informative Note 1 (sliders, gradient colour pickers, and editable areas count as one target) helps define a target but adds no requirement.

title: Language of Page
sourceQuote: The default human language of each web page can be programmatically determined
publisherCheck: For each web page in the review scope, a reviewer identifies the language that predominates in its human-readable content, then confirms that this default language is exposed in a form user agents and assistive technologies can read (for HTML, typically a valid lang value on the html element) and that the declared value matches the identified language. Repeat for every page template, locale variant, and dynamically or separately served page, since the criterion applies to each web page.
evidenceNeeded: Per page: page URL or template identifier; the human-identified predominant language of its content; the delivered markup or document metadata showing the declared default language (captured from the rendered page, not only from source templates); and a note on how a mismatch or missing declaration was ruled in or out. Locale variants each need their own record.
failureExample: A site's shared template hard-codes lang="en" on the html element, so its German-language product pages are delivered with English declared as the default language and screen readers announce the German text with English pronunciation rules.
limitation: This card records what a publisher must review; it does not assess any website. Finding a lang attribute in source or via an automated checker does not show the declared value matches the page's actual default language, nor cover every page and locale variant. Language changes of individual passages are 3.1.2, not this criterion. Status stays not-assessed.

title: Language of Parts
sourceQuote: The human language of each passage or phrase in the content can be programmatically determined except for proper names, technical terms, words of indeterminate language
publisherCheck: List every passage or phrase whose human language differs from the page default, including text in images' text alternatives, form labels, quotations, and navigation such as language-switcher links. For each one, confirm that the rendered element or an ancestor programmatically declares that language (for example a valid lang attribute in HTML) and that the declared code matches the language actually used. Exclude only proper names, technical terms, words of indeterminate language, and words or phrases that have become part of the vernacular of the immediately surrounding text, and record why each excluded item fits one of these four exceptions.
evidenceNeeded: A human-reviewed inventory of foreign-language passages and phrases per reviewed page or state, each with its location, the language actually used (confirmed by a reader of that language where needed), the programmatically determinable language from the rendered DOM or accessibility tree, and an explicit exception rationale for every unmarked item.
failureExample: An English article quotes a full French sentence in a blockquote, but neither the blockquote nor any ancestor declares lang="fr", so the quotation is exposed as English and a screen reader reads it with English pronunciation rules.
limitation: Source or automated checks can confirm that lang attributes exist and are well-formed, but not that every differing passage was found, that the declared language matches the text, or whether a word falls under an exception such as vernacular use; those need human language judgment. This card records review readiness only and never establishes that any page passes, fails, or conforms.

title: On Focus
sourceQuote: When any user interface component receives focus, it does not initiate a change of context
publisherCheck: Move focus to every user interface component on each page by keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, arrow keys within composite widgets) and by any other focus mechanism the page offers, without activating anything. For each component, record whether merely receiving focus initiates a change of context, such as opening a new window or tab, navigating to another page, submitting a form, moving focus elsewhere, or substantially changing page content that alters its meaning. Repeat for components that appear only after interaction, such as menus, dialogs, and dynamically inserted controls.
evidenceNeeded: A list of the pages and component states reviewed; for each focusable component, the focus method used and the observed result of focus alone (no activation); screen recordings or notes for any component where focus triggered navigation, a new window, form submission, focus relocation, or a major content change; and the reviewer, date, and browser or assistive technology used.
failureExample: A help link in a page footer has a script attached to its focus event that opens a new browser window as soon as a keyboard user tabs onto the link, before the user presses Enter.
limitation: This card records a manual review procedure only. Inspecting source code or running automated scanners cannot show what happens when each component actually receives focus at runtime, and no website has been evaluated here, so no claim of pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance is made.

title: On Input
sourceQuote: Changing the setting of any user interface component does not automatically cause a change of context unless the user has been advised of the behavior
publisherCheck: Inventory every user interface component whose setting a user can change (select lists, radio buttons, checkboxes, text fields, sliders, toggles). For each, change its value with keyboard and pointer without any separate submit or activation step, and record whether a change of context follows automatically (new page or window, viewport or focus moved, content changing the meaning of the page, form submitted). Where one occurs, confirm the user is advised of that behavior before using the component, and note where and how that advice is presented.
evidenceNeeded: Human-recorded list of setting-changeable components per page or state; for each, the exact input action taken, the observed result after the setting change, whether that result is a change of context, and, if so, the location and wording of the advance advice and that it is encountered before the component is used.
failureExample: A language select list navigates to the translated page as soon as a new option is highlighted with the arrow keys, with no prior advice, so keyboard users are moved away before reaching their intended choice.
limitation: Packet readiness only; no website was evaluated. Source review or automated scanning cannot establish whether a setting change triggers a change of context or whether advance advice is adequate; script handlers, assistive-technology interaction, and dynamic states need human operation. Activating controls such as links or submit buttons is not changing a setting; changes of content that are not changes of context are outside this criterion. Records observations, never a pass, fail, or conformance claim.

title: Consistent Navigation
sourceQuote: Navigational mechanisms that are repeated on multiple web pages within a set of web pages occur in the same relative order
publisherCheck: Identify the set of web pages under review and list each navigational mechanism repeated on more than one of those pages (for example main menu, breadcrumb, footer links, search, skip link). For each repeated mechanism, record the order of its items on every sampled page in both the rendered visual sequence and the programmatic reading/focus sequence, and confirm that items appearing on several pages keep the same order relative to each other. Treat a reordering as covered by the exception only when the user initiated that change (for example the user rearranged or customized the menu), and record what the user did.
evidenceNeeded: Named page set and the sampled page URLs or templates; per page, an ordered list of each repeated navigational mechanism and its items as rendered and as reached by keyboard focus or reading order; for every order difference, a note of whether a user action caused it and which action; reviewer name and review date.
failureExample: A site's header menu lists Home, Products, Support, Contact on most pages, but the Support page template renders Support, Home, Contact, Products without any user action, so the repeated menu items appear in a different relative order.
limitation: This card is a manual-review aid only and does not establish conformance; no website was evaluated. Source inspection or automated scans cannot alone show which pages form the set, which mechanisms count as repeated navigation, or whether an order change was user-initiated; rendered pages across the set need human comparison. The criterion constrains relative order of repeated mechanisms, not page-specific navigation that is not repeated.

title: Consistent Identification
sourceQuote: Components that have the same functionality within a set of web pages are identified consistently.
publisherCheck: Define the set of web pages in scope, then inventory components that perform the same function on more than one page of that set (for example search, print, download, next, close, or shared form controls). For each such function, compare how the component is identified on every page where it appears, covering its visible label, programmatic name, and any text alternative for an icon or image, and record any page where the same function is identified differently.
evidenceNeeded: A list of the pages forming the set of web pages; per repeated function, the pages and locations where its component appears; the visible label, programmatic name, and text alternative observed for each occurrence, with screenshots or accessibility-tree excerpts; and a reviewer note stating whether each occurrence truly has the same functionality.
failureExample: A documentation site shows a download icon on each article page; on most pages its text alternative is "Download PDF", but on several pages the identical icon and action are named "Get file" and "Export", so the same function is identified inconsistently across the set.
limitation: This card supports manual publisher review only; no website was evaluated and no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance is claimed. Judging same functionality and consistent identification requires human comparison across rendered pages of a defined set; source inspection or automated name matching alone cannot establish either. The criterion applies only to components with the same functionality within a set of web pages, not to single pages or components with different functions.

title: Consistent Help
sourceQuote: they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user
publisherCheck: Identify each set of web pages and list which of the four named help mechanisms (human contact details, human contact mechanism, self-help option, fully automated contact mechanism) are repeated across its pages, whether on-page or as a direct link to a help page. For each repeated mechanism, compare its position in serialized content order relative to other page content on every page in the set, holding the page variation constant (same zoom level, orientation, breakpoint). Record any order differences and whether each was caused by a user-initiated change.
evidenceNeeded: A defined page inventory for each set of web pages; per page and per page variation, the serialized (DOM/source) order of each repeated help mechanism relative to surrounding content such as header, navigation, main content and footer; the zoom, orientation and viewport used for each capture; and notes on any user action that preceded a captured state.
failureExample: Within one set of support pages, a 'Contact us' link sits in the header before the main navigation on most pages, but on the order-status page the same link is moved into the footer after the main content at the same viewport width, with no user action causing the change.
limitation: Applies only when a listed help mechanism is repeated on multiple pages within a set of web pages; it does not require any help mechanism to exist. Order differences caused by a user-initiated change (for example zoom or orientation producing a different page variation) are outside its scope. Source review or automated order comparison cannot establish the page-set boundaries or human judgement of which elements are help mechanisms, so this card records no pass, fail, applicability or conformance result.

title: Error Identification
sourceQuote: If an input error is automatically detected, the item that is in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text.
publisherCheck: For each form or input the publisher controls, list every input error the site or app detects automatically (client-side or server-side validation, including omitted required fields). For each detected error, confirm a human reviewer can find, in text, both which item is in error and a description of the error, rather than only a color change, border, icon, or generic failure notice.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of validation rules per input, plus for each automatically detected error a record of what the user is shown after triggering it: the visible text message, which item it names or is attached to, and how it is presented (inline, summary, or dialog), captured by a human on representative pages and states.
failureExample: A newsletter signup form rejects a malformed email address on submit by only turning the email field border red, with no text naming the field or explaining that the address format was not accepted.
limitation: Applies only to input errors that are automatically detected; it does not require detecting errors, suggesting corrections (see 3.3.3), or preventing errors. Source review or automated tooling alone cannot establish that every detected error state is identified and described in text; no website was evaluated, so nothing here is passed, failed, inapplicable, or conformant.

title: Labels or Instructions
sourceQuote: Labels or instructions are provided when content requires user input.
publisherCheck: List every place the content requires user input (form fields, selects, checkboxes, radio groups, date or code entry, search boxes, editable widgets). For each, confirm a label or instruction is presented to users that identifies what to enter, including any expected format or required-field indication the content depends on.
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of every user-input point on the reviewed pages and states, with a screenshot or rendered-text excerpt showing the label or instruction presented with each one, plus the reviewer name, date, page URLs and states examined.
failureExample: A newsletter signup shows a single empty text box beside a Subscribe button, with no visible label or instruction indicating that an email address is expected.
limitation: This card records a manual review prompt only; no website was evaluated. Source inspection or automated tools cannot show whether presented labels or instructions are adequate for users, so no pass, fail, inapplicability or conformance is claimed.

title: Error Suggestion
sourceQuote: If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user
publisherCheck: List every input the publisher validates automatically (client or server), including omitted required fields and values outside an accepted format or range. For each validation rule, record whether the system knows a correction (an accepted format, allowed values, range, or a likely intended value). Where a correction is known, trigger the error with benign test data and confirm the message presented to the user states that correction in text, not only that the input is wrong. Where no suggestion is shown, record the publisher's stated reason and check it is that a suggestion would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content (for example, revealing which part of a login credential was wrong, or giving away a test answer).
evidenceNeeded: An inventory of automatically detected input errors per form or control, the validation rule each applies, and whether a correction is known; the exact error text shown for each, captured from the rendered interface after a benign invalid entry; and, for each rule where a known correction is withheld, a written security or purpose rationale reviewed by a human.
failureExample: A delivery-date field rejects "31/12/2026" because the form only accepts YYYY-MM-DD, but the only message shown is "Invalid date"; the expected format is known to the validator yet is never suggested to the user.
limitation: Applies only to errors that are automatically detected and whose corrections are known; it does not require detecting errors or inventing suggestions. The security-or-purpose exception needs human judgment. Source review or automated scans cannot show the rendered message wording or whether a suggestion was withheld legitimately, so this card records review readiness only and makes no conformance claim for any website.

title: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
sourceQuote: A mechanism is available for reviewing, confirming, and correcting information before finalizing the submission.
publisherCheck: Inventory every page or step that causes a legal commitment or financial transaction for the user, modifies or deletes user-controllable data in a data storage system, or submits user test responses. For each, record which of the three options holds: the submission is reversible; user-entered data is checked for input errors and the user is given an opportunity to correct them; or a mechanism lets the user review, confirm, and correct information before the submission is finalized. Pages outside those four triggers are not in scope for this criterion; record the reason they were excluded rather than marking them as passed.
evidenceNeeded: A list of in-scope submission flows naming the trigger each one matches (legal, financial, modify/delete stored user data, test responses). For each flow, the option relied on (reversible, checked, or confirmed) and human-observed evidence that it works: for reversible, the cancel or undo path and any time limit on it; for checked, the input-error messages and the correction opportunity; for confirmed, the review step showing the entered information with controls to correct it and to confirm before finalizing. Include the reviewer's name, the date, and the page or build version reviewed.
failureExample: An account settings page has a single "Delete my saved addresses" button that permanently removes the stored addresses as soon as it is activated. There is no confirmation step, no chance to correct the selection, and no way to restore the addresses afterward.
limitation: This card is publisher review guidance only; no website was evaluated, and source text or automated checks cannot show conformance. Whether a flow is in scope, and whether a reversal, error check, or review step actually works for users, needs a human to work through the real flow. Meeting any one of the three options satisfies the criterion's requirement for that flow, but this card makes no claim about any other success criterion or about overall conformance.

title: Redundant Entry
sourceQuote: required to be entered again in the same process is either: auto-populated, or available for the user to select.
publisherCheck: List each multi-step process, such as checkout, registration, or an application form. For each step, record every field asking for information the user already entered or was given earlier in the same process. For each such field, confirm that the earlier value is auto-populated or offered for selection, for example through a 'same as shipping address' option or a choice list of earlier entries. Where neither is offered, record which exception the publisher relies on: re-entry is essential, the information is needed to ensure the security of the content, or the earlier information is no longer valid. Record the reason for that exception.
evidenceNeeded: A step-by-step walkthrough of each process, made by a human, with screenshots or notes of the fields at each step. A mapping from each repeated field to the earlier step where the same information was entered or provided. The mechanism observed for each repeated field: auto-populated, selectable, or none. For each field without a mechanism, a written justification naming the exception that applies.
failureExample: A checkout collects the shipping address on step 1. On step 3 it asks for the billing address in blank fields, with no option to reuse the shipping address and no prefilled values. The user has to type the same address again.
limitation: Readiness record only; status stays not-assessed. Source review or automated scans cannot establish which fields repeat within one process, whether values actually prefill, or whether an essential, security, or no-longer-valid exception legitimately applies; only a human walkthrough of each live process can. Information from a different process is outside this criterion's scope. This card declares no pass, fail, inapplicability, or conformance.

title: Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
sourceQuote: A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle) is not required for any step in an authentication process
publisherCheck: List every step of each authentication process the publisher offers (sign-in, step-up verification, account recovery). For each step that requires a cognitive function test, such as recalling a password or solving a puzzle, record which of the four listed provisions that step provides: an Alternative authentication method that does not rely on a cognitive function test; a Mechanism assisting the user in completing the test; a test to recognize objects; or a test to identify non-text content the user provided to the website. A step requiring a cognitive function test with none of these four is a candidate finding for a human reviewer.
evidenceNeeded: A human-compiled inventory of authentication steps per process, naming the cognitive function test (if any) at each step and the specific provision relied on. For a Mechanism claim, record how it assists the user, for example whether password fields accept password-manager autofill and pasting, which the criterion's informative Note 2 gives as examples. For Object Recognition or Personal Content claims, record what the user must recognize or identify; Note 1 says these may be images, video, or audio. For an Alternative claim, record that the alternative method itself does not rely on a cognitive function test.
failureExample: A sign-in form's password field blocks paste and disables autofill, so the user must recall and retype the password, and no other sign-in method that avoids a cognitive function test is offered at that step.
limitation: Source reading or automated scanning cannot establish this criterion: it depends on every step of every authentication process, including flows behind accounts and conditional verification steps, and on whether a provision actually assists the user. No website was evaluated; this card is a manual-review prompt only and does not state that any website passes, fails, or conforms. The saved normative text does not define 'cognitive function test'; reviewers should consult the WCAG 2.2 glossary rather than infer one.

title: Name, Role, Value
sourceQuote: the name and role can be programmatically determined
publisherCheck: List every user interface component on the reviewed pages, including form elements, links, and script-generated or custom widgets. For each, use the accessibility tree or an assistive technology to confirm that a name and a role are exposed. For components with user-settable states, properties, or values (for example checked, expanded, selected, or slider value), confirm they can be set programmatically. Then confirm that changes to these items are announced to or detectable by user agents, including assistive technologies, after the user interacts with the component.
evidenceNeeded: A per-page inventory of user interface components, with special attention to custom or script-generated ones. For each component, record its exposed name, role, and relevant states, properties, or values as reported by an accessibility inspector or assistive technology, before and after interaction. Also record the tooling and versions used, the pages and states reviewed, and who reviewed them.
failureExample: A custom disclosure toggle built from a scripted div shows a chevron icon and expands a panel when clicked. However, it exposes no name, no button role, and no expanded or collapsed state, so a screen reader user hears nothing meaningful and is not told that the panel opened.
limitation: This card is a manual-review prompt; it does not test any website. Reading source code or running automated checkers alone cannot confirm that names, roles, states, and change notifications are actually exposed to assistive technologies at runtime. The criterion applies to all user interface components. The non-normative note says it mainly concerns authors who build or script their own components, and that standard HTML controls already meet it when used according to specification; misused or ARIA-modified native controls still need review.

title: Status Messages
sourceQuote: status messages can be programmatically determined through role or properties such that they can be presented to the user by assistive technologies without receiving focus
publisherCheck: Prepare an inventory of content changes implemented in markup that report an action's result, a waiting state, progress, or errors without changing context. Distinguish WCAG-defined status messages from changes of context using the normative glossary. For each in-scope message, request a separately authorized browser and assistive-technology evaluation to determine whether its role or properties allow presentation without receiving focus. The evaluator records the exposed semantics, focus behavior and relevant accessibility-support evidence. Specific ARIA roles and implementation sequences are possible techniques, not additional requirements of this criterion; this packet performs no browser or account operation.
evidenceNeeded: A list of each status message with the triggering user action and its location; DOM snapshots before and after the trigger showing the role or live-region attributes on the container and the inserted text; a note of where focus was before and after; and a screen reader transcript or recording (product and version, browser and version) showing the announcement occurred without focus moving.
failureExample: On a newsletter signup form, pressing Subscribe inserts 'Thanks, you are subscribed' into a plain div with no role or aria-live attribute and leaves focus on the button, so a screen reader user hears nothing and does not learn the request succeeded.
limitation: This card records a manual review procedure only; no website was evaluated and no pass, fail, or conformance claim is made. Source inspection or automated scanners can show that live-region roles or attributes exist, but cannot establish which content changes are status messages, whether every one is covered, or whether assistive technologies actually announce them without focus. The criterion applies only to content implemented using markup languages and only to changes that are status messages, not to changes of context or messages delivered by moving focus.
